title: One-to-One and Onto Functions
short: One-to-one: different inputs give different outputs. Onto: every element of the codomain is reached.
trouble: Students decide without looking at the domain and codomain, but f(x) = x² is one-to-one and onto from [0, ∞) to [0, ∞) and neither from the real numbers to the real numbers.

blocks.html: Two questions about any function come up again and again: does it ever send two inputs to the same place, and does it reach everything in its codomain? The answers decide whether the function can be undone, and they power many counting arguments.

$f : A \to B$ is one-to-one (injective) when different inputs always give different outputs: $f(a_{1}) = f(a_{2})$ implies $a_{1} = a_{2}$. It is onto (surjective) when every element of $B$ is an output: for every $b \in B$ there is an $a \in A$ with $f(a) = b$. A function that is both is a bijection.

In an arrow diagram: one-to-one means no dot of $B$ receives two arrows; onto means every dot of $B$ receives at least one. For finite sets this gives a size check. A one-to-one function needs at least as many outputs as inputs, so $|A| \le |B|$; an onto function needs enough inputs to cover the outputs, so $|A| \ge |B|$; and a bijection forces $|A| = |B|$. Both properties depend on the domain and codomain, not just the formula.

blocks.name: disc-relation
blocks.cap: $x \mapsto x^{2}$ on $\{-2, \ldots, 2\}$. Rings mark outputs hit twice (not one-to-one) and outputs never hit (not onto). Switch the codomain to "outputs only": the function becomes onto, though still not one-to-one.

head: $f(x) = x^{2}$
one-to-one?
onto?
blocks.cap: The formula $x^{2}$ with four choices of domain and codomain.

blocks.title: Proving one-to-one, disproving onto
steps: One-to-one: suppose $f(a) = f(b)$. Then $2a + 1 = 2b + 1$, so $2a = 2b$ and $a = b$. Yes.
Onto: is $2$ an output? $2n + 1 = 2$ gives $n = \frac{1}{2}$, not an integer. So $2$ is never reached: not onto.
Over the real numbers, $f(x) = 2x + 1$ is onto ($x = \frac{y - 1}{2}$), so the same formula is a bijection $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$.

blocks.title: Counting one-to-one functions
blocks.q: How many one-to-one functions are there from a $3$-element set to a $5$-element set?
steps: The first input has $5$ choices of output.
The second must avoid the first output: $4$ choices. The third: $3$ choices.

blocks.html: Deciding without looking at the domain and codomain. "Is $x^{2}$ one-to-one?" has no answer until you know the sets: the table above shows all four combinations happening. Check: to show "not one-to-one," name two inputs with the same output; to show "not onto," name an element of the codomain that no input reaches.
